doc.title: Christine Jensen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 4, 2024

title: Learning with records then versus today's media; the Nat King Cole listening test
summary: She contrasts learning from records and cassettes with today's flood of media, and tells how a student's blind test with Lester Young, Buddy Rich and Nat King Cole humbled her.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you think the access that they have now to just about everything in all the different media is a positive or negative to them learning the music and specifically learning to use their ear?

I want to say positive. There’s some negative because it’s not far off — I mean what a crazy thing — I now get to say I’m from a generation where when I was learning there was no cell phones, there was no internet connection, there was no media. All we had were records and tapes and cassettes and 50% slowdown playback. And hopefully the resources landed in front of us from someone that was able to share, I don’t know, the right way to sift through a library or a record store or something, for us to get the information in front of us, right? And even before me, my generation, all they had were records. And before that generation all they had was piano player rolls probably. You

know what I mean? All of it is a learning tool that is very strong. And it’s kind of about sifting through it. Now they just have way more to sift through, just like media. We have way more to sift through. And it’s easy to get things covered up. It’s funny because a student of mine played me, he did a listening test on me and I completely failed it. It was Lester Young, Buddy Rich and guess the piano player. You’d never guess the piano player. And it was a trio from like 1942.

Playing the crap out of the piano, like I was just like — you know I grew up with lots of Nat King Cole but it was the more popular Nat King Cole and now I’m like this guy set the bar for everybody off this recording from 1942 or whatever year it was, of a trio — a bass-less trio.

And it’s like where have I been like what did I miss? You know what I mean? In the lineage of the whole thing. So what are they missing now I don’t know. I mean I think — some things I think are the same, like the hippest thing going. For me the hippest thing going was Branford Marsalis and Sting and Wynton and a bunch of things. Now they have this thing going it’s still Brad Mehldau and I don’t know who are the younger cats. I guess the piano player — all these names are going to escape me right now — but there’s the swing to — in instrumental jazz anyway — toward whatever the new kid on the — it was Roy Hargrove for the longest time. They’re still listening to Roy Hargrove. I’m like that’s great but man there’s so much history in Roy’s playing coming from the masters. So I think that’s the great thing about education is that we do get to share some reality checks on the history and the pedagogy of the music in a learning space. And I’m so afraid because I just hope that these learning spaces continue to exist because the world is getting swallowed up by a lot of other things that are much more negative.
